name: Search design and model choice: one prompt with the whole catalog (today) versus request-to-tags, code scoring and LLM re-rank of a shortlist; Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus through claude -p
what_it_is: A decision about how server/vibe.ts turns a request into 15-20 fonts. Option 1 (today): all 2,099 catalog rows in one cached system prompt (166,277 characters) and one `claude -p` call that returns two lists with a reason per pick. Option 2: a small first call turns the request into weights over Google tags and shape traits, plain code scores every row, a second call re-ranks 60-100 shortlisted rows. Option 3 (recommended below): keep option 1 as the recall engine and add code around it (model and effort choice, row order, output length, fairness for untagged rows, hard filters, a taste term for the user's shortlist). Also covers model choice (Haiku 4.5 now; Sonnet 5.5, Opus) and how the user's shortlist and culled fonts should weigh against the request.
provider_and_url: Anthropic: models overview https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview ; prompt caching https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching ; model deprecations https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations ; prompting guide (long context) https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices ; Claude Code CLI reference https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference , model config https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config , env vars https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars , headless mode https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless . Research: Liu et al., 'Lost in the Middle', https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172 ; Sun et al., 'Is ChatGPT Good at Search?' (RankGPT), https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.09542 ; 'Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval', https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05381 ; Rocchio feedback weights, https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/the-rocchio71-algorithm-1.html .
catalog_coverage: Option 1 sees all 2,099 rows (Google 1,760, Fontshare 64, Velvetyne 63, Collletttivo 26, Tunera 23, Use & Modify 163). A tag-scoring step can score only rows that have Google-vocabulary tags: 1,611 of 1,760 Google families (1,523 flat + 88 axis-position only) and none of the 339 non-Google families; 149 Google families have no mood row at all (counted by me, see the indie-gap item). In option 1 the 339 non-Google rows still compete through the foundries' own words, in option 2 they cannot be scored until they are labelled.
granularity: Per family: one line per family, no style, italic or axis information. A scoring step could add per-style numbers (slant, weight, width) but that is a data question for the measured-traits item.
signal_type: Semantic: tags, foundry words, category and the model's memory of what named typefaces look like. The model never sees letters; shape enters only through tags and memory.
mood_dimensions_covered: Measured by me with the app's real prompt (evidence/build_prompts.ts, run_claude.mjs; 2026-10-03; request-only user prompt, no wordmark line). Precision = share of the run's Google picks whose own Google tag is >= 60 (Google rows only; foundry rows have no Google tag). Pixel (43 positives): Haiku 8 of 8, Sonnet 5.5 12 of 12; with Google tags hidden still 4 of 5 and 11 of 12, so names alone carry it. Blackletter (16 positives): Haiku 5 of 7, Sonnet 9 of 12 (hidden: 3 of 6 and 5 of 10). Loud (155): Haiku 6 of 12, Sonnet 4 of 8 (hidden Haiku: no Google pick at all; Sonnet 4 of 9). Calm (247): Haiku 4 of 13, Sonnet 1 of 6; the prompt tells the model to avoid 'very common' fonts (58 of the 247 Calm positives are), and its idea of calm is a distinctive face, not Google's. Motion ('fonts that imply fast movement or action'): Google Active >= 60 in 0-4 of about 12 Haiku Google picks (six runs: 2, 2, 3, 0, 4, 0) and 2-3 of about 9 Sonnet Google picks (five runs: 3, 2, 3, 3, 3). The picks are wide, heavy racing and techno faces (Racing Sans One, Faster One, Orbitron, Audiowide, Syncopate, Michroma, Sporting Grotesque, Outward, Nippo); of the 12 Google picks with legacy metrics the mean width is 7.5 against 6.5 for the catalog (z = 2.2) and slant is not raised (1.6 vs 1.7). Google's Active tag marks something else (script and comic display, mean legacy slant 5.1 for Active >= 60 fonts), so Active-based silver labels disagree with the model by meaning, not by error. Futuristic: 6 and 8 of the Google picks of the two first Haiku motion runs carry Futuristic >= 60.
query_style_specificity: Tight literal requests (pixel, blackletter) are close to solved by names plus tags. Loose or abstract ones (calm, fast, friendly) are where runs disagree: for 'fast movement or action' two identical Haiku runs share only 19% of picks on average and Sonnet 5.5 (low effort) 50%. The two-stage tag-only shortlist is best at tag-faithful requests and worst at motion (see quality_evidence).
quality_evidence: All numbers below are measured by me unless marked; about 54 `claude -p` calls over 35 minutes, files in docs/research/font-vibe-search/results/evidence/ (live-runs.jsonl holds every pick list and usage record). Small samples: treat as direction, not proof. (1) Repeatability, 'fast movement or action', same prompt: Haiku 4.5 n=6 mean pairwise Jaccard of picks 0.19 (range 0.03-0.34; 41 of 71 distinct picks appeared in one run only); Sonnet 5.5 low effort n=5 mean 0.50 (0.29-0.67). Across models 0.03-0.30. (2) Model comparison: Sonnet 5.5 low picks Active >= 60 fonts a little more steadily (hits per run 3, 2, 3, 3, 3 vs Haiku 2, 2, 3, 0, 4, 0) and on four literal/mood queries had 68% precision against Google's tags vs Haiku's 57.5% (26 of 38 vs 23 of 40 Google picks; tiny n). (3) Tags hidden from all 1,760 Google rows: Haiku fell to 40% (8 of 20) and picked about half as many Google fonts; Sonnet fell to 53% (20 of 38) and kept its Google share. Sonnet leans less on visible tags. (4) Position bias, shipped order (indie, Fontshare, then Google by popularity with 'very common' last): over 10 matched query/model runs (5 requests x Haiku and Sonnet low) only 11% of Google picks (11 of 98) came from deciles 6-8 of the Google block against 30% if uniform, while the first and last decile took 36%. With the Google block shuffled (seed 1, same 10 runs) the shares were 25% (29 of 117) and 24%, and silver precision did not drop (54 of 98 = 55% sorted vs 63 of 117 = 54% shuffled). Consistent with Liu et al. (2023): accuracy highest at the start and end, and in their test GPT-3.5 fell by over 20% for middle positions; confounded here by popularity order, runs not independent. (5) Tag-only two-stage shortlist: Haiku turns the request into Google-tag weights in 2.2-3.2 s (1.2k tokens in, 205-341 out; weights stable: Active 1.0, Excited 0.9, Innovative 0.5-0.6, Loud 0.5-0.6, Calm -0.8, Stiff -0.7). Scoring all 1,611 taggable Google families with those weights, the top 80 contained only 11% and 20% (two weight sets) of the Google fonts the whole-catalog runs picked, the top 200 23-33%, the top 400 33-48% (random 5%, 12%, 25%). The tag-ranked top 20 were comic and bubble display faces (Kablammo, Kavoon, Climate Crisis, Mogra, Luckiest Guy, Bangers); 15-17 of 20 had Active >= 60. A tag-first design would drop most of what the LLM finds by knowing what 'fast' looks like. (6) Literature (not re-run): Liu et al. 2023 found a U-shaped use of long contexts; 'Context Length Alone Hurts' (2025) reports 14-85% drops with length alone; RankGPT-style listwise re-ranking works on 20-document windows sliding by 10 over a first-stage top 100 and beat a fine-tuned monoT5-3B by 2.7 nDCG with GPT-4. Anthropic's guide says to put long data at the top and the query at the end ('up to 30 percent' better in their tests), which vibe.ts already does. [uncertain]
known_noise: Run-to-run variation is large (above) and cannot be tuned away: claude -p has no temperature flag and Opus 4.7+/Sonnet 5.x reject non-default sampling parameters. Haiku often answers twice (a structured-output call, then a text copy): usage showed two API iterations in 8 of 23 Haiku runs, mean wall 16.2 s against 10.3 s for single-iteration runs; Sonnet 5.5 did it in 0 of 24 runs. One Haiku run (1 of 24 Haiku runs, 0 of 24 Sonnet runs, all with my request-only prompt) refused and asked for the wordmark; likely an artifact of my prompts, the app always sends a wordmark line. Instruction leakage: the prompt says to avoid 'very common' fonts, yet 18% of Google picks (18 of 98 in the matched sorted-order runs) came from the last 10% of the Google block, which holds the 172 very common fonts (9.8% of rows).
name_and_memory_bias: Large for literal themes, small for moods. Crude name lexicon: 72% of Google Pixel positives carry a pixel-type word in their name, against 14% of Futuristic, 20% of Techno, 8% of Active. With Google tags hidden, Haiku's silver precision fell from 57.5% to 40% and Sonnet's from 68% to 53%, so most of the remaining hits come from names and memory. The reasons the model gives ('squared counters and a wide stance') are plausible but come from memory of named fonts, not from letters it can see.
untagged_rows: Silently pushed down, measured. With Google tags hidden (a stand-in for untagged rows) and foundry rows still tagged, Haiku picked 5.2 Google fonts per run instead of 12.2 for the motion request, and 0 of 21 picks were Google fonts for 'loud, shouting, impossible to ignore'. Sonnet 5.5 low barely moved (8.4 vs 9.0 Google picks per run). Indie rows also get a head start: the 275 libre-foundry rows (13% of the catalog) sit first in the prompt and the instructions demand 6-8 'independent' picks, so 4-16 of 15-24 picks per run were indie (mean 42%). In option 2 untagged rows would score zero and could not be shortlisted at all.
text_interference_risk: Not a visual method. The wordmark text is only a string in the user prompt; the model cannot see how it sets.
integration_path: Option 3 changes, in order of value. (a) Model and effort in askClaudeCode (and, for Haiku, avoid the double answer that cost 6 s in 8 of 23 runs, e.g. by telling it to reply only through the structured-output tool): for Sonnet 5.5 or Opus 5.x add `--effort low`; MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 does not turn thinking off on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 or Fable (Claude Code docs) and Sonnet at default effort spent 883 thinking tokens and 16.3 s in my run; keep MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 for Haiku. Add `--fallback-model sonnet` (documented chain flag) because Haiku 4.5's retirement is 'not sooner than 2026-10-15'. (b) Shorter output: reasons only for the first 8 picks of each list; output tokens set latency (about 95 tokens/s on both models, wall = output/95 + ~1.5 s). (c) Row order: a fixed seeded shuffle of the Google block keeps the cache stable and removes the measured U-shape; or place code-scored candidates at the start and end. (d) Fairness for untagged rows: give them a label line in Google's vocabulary (see indie-gap) and/or a code-side floor so a font with no tags is not outscored by tag text. (e) User candidates in code, not prose: culled = hard filter (already in mergePicks) plus at most the 10 most recent names in the prompt; shortlist = at most 8 most recent as taste exemplars with their tags, plus a taste vector in code for tie-breaks. Starting weights from Rocchio feedback (Manning et al.: alpha 1 request, beta 0.75 liked, gamma 0.15 disliked; positive feedback is worth more than negative); treat as untested here [uncertain]. For 'more like #3' the anchor font's profile replaces the text query. (f) Optional stage 1 as an extra recall channel, not a gate: JSON {"tags":{"Active":1.0,"Excited":0.9,"Calm":-0.8},"traits":{"width":"wide","weight":"heavy","slant":"any"}} from a 1.2k-token Haiku call, code scores the rows it can (tags now, traits when measured), the top 60 are merged with the LLM's picks. Use alone only for tag-faithful requests (pixel, brush, blackletter, techno, calm, loud). (g) Cache the result per (query, constraints, catalog version, model) so a repeated request returns the same grid; add an explicit 'new draw' action. [uncertain]
tokens_per_row: Measured from usage fields: 57,008 prompt tokens on Haiku 4.5 for 2,099 rows (27 per row, 2.92 characters per token; the 3.5 chars/token estimate in server/check-vibe.ts undercounts tokens by about 17%), 76,984-77,011 on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5 (37 per row; the newer tokenizer gives about 35% more tokens, matching Anthropic's '555k vs 750k words per 1M tokens'). Google tag text is 73,203 of 166,277 characters (25.2k Haiku tokens, 44%); the variant without Google tags is 93,074 characters (31.8k Haiku tokens, 41.5k Sonnet). Adding two-digit weights to six tags per Google row would add about 10.8k tokens (+19%); dropping the 172 'very common' rows would save about 4.7k. A stage-2 shortlist of 60-100 rows is about 2-4k tokens and needs no cache. The prompt is cached as one block: any edit rewrites it once (the shared 29k-character prefix appeared not to be reused when I changed later lines); the cache lifetime was 1 hour on this login (usage showed ephemeral_1h tokens), so bursts of searches within an hour read it at 10% price.
vocabulary_alignment: Option 1 mixes Google's tags (Google rows), foundry words (indie rows), Fontshare use cases, plus 'very common'; the model bridges them from memory, which is why indie rows without Google moods lose. A stage-1 translator needs a closed vocabulary: the 33 Google tag names worked in 2 of 2 runs with correct names. Motion has no Google tag, so it needs shape traits.
explainability: Option 1: the model's one-line reasons (under 14 words) are fluent rationales from memory, not measurements. Option 2: code can show the matched tags and weights or measured trait values, which is checkable; the re-rank reasons are again from the model.
determinism: Not deterministic and not controllable. Identical prompt, same model, 'fast movement or action': mean pairwise overlap 0.19 (Haiku, 6 runs), 0.50 (Sonnet 5.5 low, 5 runs). Option 2's code scoring is deterministic given the stage-1 weights (stage 1 itself varied a little: Futuristic 0.7 in one run, Rugged 0.4 in the other). Caching results per request gives repeatability at the cost of fresh draws.
build_effort: (a)-(c), (g): half a day for an agent in this codebase, including the A/B run. (d): depends on the indie-gap work. (e): a day with tests. (f) stage 1 plus tag scoring plus merge: 1-2 days; traits scoring waits on measured traits for all rows. Evaluation harness: see evaluation item.
per_search_cost_and_latency: Measured on this Max login, claude 2.1.274, 2026-10-03, full catalog prompt, two lists with reasons. A do-nothing `claude -p` call (340-token prompt, Haiku) takes 1.7 s wall (0.6 s API, about 1.1 s CLI start). Haiku 4.5: n=15 wall mean 11.7 s (median 11.9, range 7.7-18.0), output mean 1,088 tokens (680-1,832). Sonnet 5.5 `--effort low`: n=14 mean 9.6 s (6.7-14.9), output 808 tokens (724-870, very consistent). Sonnet 5.5 at default effort: 16.3 s with 883 thinking tokens (n=1). Opus 5 (tried because Opus 5.5 failed) low effort: 14.2 s, 736 tokens (n=1); Opus 5.5 returned HTTP 400 because the installed CLI needs 2.1.280 or newer. Two-stage estimate (stage 1 measured 3.3-4.4 s wall; stage 2 estimated from throughput): about 10-13 s, so it does not beat Sonnet low on speed; it cuts input from 57-77k cached tokens to about 4k and removes the cache dependency. Subscription: no dollars per search, but usage counts against the Max plan limits (not documented in what I read; Sonnet 5.5 and Opus read about 35% more tokens than Haiku) [uncertain]. API-equivalent at published prices, cached: Haiku about $0.011 per search (57k reads at $0.10/MTok plus 1,088 output tokens at $5/MTok), Sonnet 5.5 about $0.024 (77k at $0.20/MTok plus 808 at $10/MTok). A cache write at the 1-hour rate is about $0.11 (Haiku) or $0.31 (Sonnet), paid once per prompt change per hour. Claude Code's own total_cost_usd for Sonnet 5.5 ($0.81 for the first call) is wrong because the installed CLI prints 'unrecognized_model'; ignore it. [uncertain]
one_off_cost: My measurements: about 54 `claude -p` calls, roughly $2-4 API-equivalent, nothing billed on the subscription; scripts and outputs in docs/research/font-vibe-search/results/evidence/. The recommended A/B (25 requests x 3 variants x 2 replicates = 150 searches, about 25 minutes sequential, one cache write per variant) is of similar size.
human_effort: None to build. Judging the result of a model or ordering change needs a rating round: about 17-38 minutes (see evaluation item).
asset_access: No external assets. Needs the `claude` CLI signed in to the subscription (`--safe-mode`, as vibe.ts uses; `--bare` does not use subscription login and needs an API key). The installed CLI is 2.1.274: it runs claude-sonnet-5-5 but prints an unrecognized-model warning, and cannot run claude-opus-5-5 (needs >= 2.1.280); updating it is the user's call and I did not run `claude update`.
licence_and_provenance: Personal use of the user's own Claude subscription through the documented `claude -p` / `claude setup-token` path. Plan limits apply and I found no documented per-plan numbers for scripted runs [uncertain]. The static export has no vibe search, so nothing is redistributed. [uncertain]
etiquette: Keep searches sequential or lightly parallel; my 54 calls over 35 minutes hit no limit. Do not loop evaluation runs unattended without a cap (claude -p has --max-turns; --max-budget-usd counts client-side cost estimates, which are wrong for models the installed CLI does not recognise).
maintenance_and_freshness: Model lifecycle matters now: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 is Active but its tentative retirement is 'not sooner than October 15, 2026' (12 days after today, 2026-10-03; Anthropic promises at least 60 days' notice and I saw no deprecation notice); claude-sonnet-4-5 is deprecated (retires 2026-11-30); Sonnet 5.5 was released 2026-09-28. The app pins the dated Haiku id; `--fallback-model` or an alias (`haiku`) avoids a hard failure. Catalog or tag edits rewrite the cache once. Any change in `claude` version or default effort can shift latency and thinking.
risks_and_limitations: 1) Everything above is small-sample and used a request-only user prompt (no wordmark, brief, history), so real searches will differ somewhat. 2) Google's tags are a partial oracle: 'Active' is not 'fast', and 89-100% of silver positives are already visible in the prompt (Active 89%, Loud 93%, Calm 100%), so scoring the current system against them is circular. 3) Moving to a tag-first pipeline would lose most of the LLM's picks on motion requests (top-80 recall 11-20%). 4) Sonnet 5.5 and Opus read about 35% more tokens and cannot have thinking switched off; effort low is the lever; quota draw unknown. 5) The position effect is confounded with popularity order. 6) Opus 5.5 and Fable were not tested (CLI too old; Fable is slower, $10/$50 per MTok, and may bill to usage credits on Max per Claude Code docs).
evaluation_hook: Replicates per query to get a noise floor (self-overlap), hidden-tag runs to measure fairness, shuffled-order runs to measure position, and blind A/B grids rated by the person (see evaluation item).
recommendation_for_font_explorer: Keep the single whole-catalog prompt as the recall engine and wrap code around it; do not move to tag-first scoring now. Evidence: the tag-scored top 80 recovers only 11-20% of what the model picks for a motion request, because Google has no speed tag and its Active tag means lively script. Model: try Sonnet 5.5 with `--effort low` against Haiku 4.5 in one rating round. In my runs it was as fast (9.6 s vs 11.7 s mean), 2.6x more repeatable (0.50 vs 0.19 overlap), less dependent on visible tags (53% vs 40% silver precision when hidden), at about 35% more input tokens and unknown quota draw. Opus and Fable add latency and cost with no evidence of gain for a pick-from-list task; not recommended for an interactive search. Whatever you choose, add `--fallback-model` because Haiku 4.5's retirement date is near. Smallest first step (an hour): in askClaudeCode add `--effort low` for non-Haiku models, drop reasons after the 8th pick, and shuffle the Google block with a fixed seed; rerun the 25-request set (evaluation item) twice per variant and compare overlap, wall time and the person's A/B votes. Second step: fairness for untagged rows (indie-gap item) and the user-candidate changes in (e). Third, optional: stage 1 as an extra recall channel for tag-faithful requests, once shape traits exist; it buys determinism and cost, not speed.
